strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly articulates genuine limitations in existing brain foundation models (conflation of time/frequency, lack of spatial awareness, computational inefficiency) with principled neuroscience-grounded solutions
Massive scale and comprehensive pretraining: 28,000 hours of EEG from 9 diverse datasets covering 17,000+ subjects, with four model variants (57M-1.9B parameters) and thorough scaling law analysis

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluation on 9 downstream tasks spanning clinical diagnosis, emotion recognition, BCI, cognitive tasks; dual protocols (linear probing and fine-tuning); multiple metrics; detailed ablation studies
Consistent and strong empirical results: SOTA performance across all 9 benchmarks with often substantial improvements (e.g., TUAB: 0.8197 vs 0.8172 for CSBrain, but note fairness concerns)
Excellent reproducibility documentation: Detailed hyperparameters in appendices (Tables 8-11), dataset information (Tables 6-7), pseudocode for core components, and code availability promise

Thoughtful architectural design: Multi-domain processing (time/frequency/raw) with cross-attention fusion, hierarchical topological embeddings, MoE for specialization and efficiency, dual-domain reconstruction objective
Systematic ablation study: Tables 4-5 demonstrate meaningful contribution of each component, with HFPM providing largest single improvement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are established techniques (time/frequency decomposition, cross-attention, MoE from Switch Transformers, RoPE positional encoding, MAE-style masked autoencoding). Main contribution is thoughtful combination rather than novel methods, limiting impact for top-tier AI venues

Topological embedding under-specified and generalization unclear: Mechanism for unifying different electrode standards is vague; no clear explanation of how variable electrode counts (4-23 channels across datasets) are handled; reference to 'standard neuroanatomical template' is underspecified; conceptual justification in Appendix D.2 is insufficient

Unclear technical details: (1) Raw path encoder claimed as 'lossless reference' but is just linear projection—how is losslessness enforced?; (2) Topological embedding parameter count and impact on model size not quantified; (3) Train/val/test split for 28k-hour corpus not specified; (4) Handling of dataset imbalance (TUEG: 27,100h vs. Raw EEG: 34.35h) not addressed

MoE contribution appears modest and under-analyzed: Ablation shows MoE alone provides minimal improvement (≤0.02 AUROC); significant gain only in combination with other components; no evidence of claimed specialization—no analysis of which experts route to which signal patterns or EEG components

Baseline comparison fairness concerns: CSBrain results marked as externally reported (not open-source), raising potential reporting bias concerns; some task-specific baselines dated (2018-2022); NeuroLM-XL and EEGPT only compared in 'pretrained only' mode in some tables

Overclaimed interpretability: Abstract claims 'interpretable representations' but evidence limited to t-SNE visualization; no attention visualizations, expert routing analysis, or systematic interpretability evaluation
Missing statistical significance testing: Standard deviations provided but no t-tests or confidence intervals; improvements sometimes modest and potentially within error margins

Incomplete computational analysis: No reporting of training cost (1.9B params on 32 A100s for 50 epochs), inference latency, or memory requirements—important for reproducibility and practical deployment

Limited application scope: Evaluation restricted to classification tasks only; no regression, anomaly detection, or other EEG applications; all tasks short-duration clinical/BCI scenarios; generalization to long-duration monitoring or novel domains unclear
Missing failure analysis and error study: No discussion of tasks/datasets where model underperforms; no qualitative failure cases or error analysis; when and why does the model struggle?
Unspecified loss weight selection: Dual-domain loss weights (λ_T=0.8, λ_F=0.2) appear fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis; how were these values chosen?
Presentation issues: Figure 2 extremely dense and difficult to parse; key technical details relegated to appendices (D.1-D.2) that should be in main paper for clarity

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying real limitations of existing EEG foundation models (time/frequency conflation, ignored spatial topology)
Comprehensive evaluation across 9 diverse downstream tasks spanning clinical diagnosis, emotion recognition, and motor imagery
Large-scale pretraining on 28,000 hours of EEG data from 9 datasets demonstrates serious engineering effort
Systematic ablation studies (Tables 4-5) validate component contributions
Scaling law experiments (Appendix G) provide insight into model/data dependencies
Thorough documentation and promise of code release support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: all components are standard techniques (time-frequency decomposition, positional embeddings, MoE, masked autoencoding) applied without significant innovation

Weak justification for design choices: (1) spatial topology encoding uncriticized despite unclear benefit; (2) dual-domain loss appears ad-hoc without ablation; (3) MoE claims specialization unsupported by analysis of expert routing

Potentially unfair experimental comparisons: overlapping pretraining/evaluation datasets (TUEG-TUAB, SEED), task-specific baselines not designed for zero-shot, other foundation models likely use different pretraining data

Scaling law results contradict core claims: 1.9B model underperforms 800M parameters (Table 12: 0.6568 vs 0.6629 Balanced Acc), suggesting scalability issues rather than continued improvement with size
Large linear probing to fine-tuning gaps (e.g., TUAB: 0.7844→0.8197) indicate weak universal representations; most improvements from task-specific adaptation rather than pretraining
Statistical significance concerns: many reported improvements are 1-2% with overlapping error bars (e.g., Table 1 TUAB Balanced Acc between Uni-NTFMlarge and LaBraM-Base); no significance tests

Critical technical detail obscured: mapping of diverse electrode configurations to standard neuroanatomical template inadequately explained; Appendix D.2 assumes regular grid structure unrealistic for actual EEG

Limited insight into learned representations: no analysis of whether spatial embeddings capture brain structure, whether MoE experts specialize, or what drives improvements; t-SNE visualization alone insufficient
Incomplete ablations: only on 2/9 tasks (TUAB, TUEV); missing ablations on loss weights, alternative spatial encodings, masking strategies

Presentation and terminology issues: 'Unified' doesn't unify electrode standards (just uses learnable embeddings); 'universal' overstated (only EEG, all classification); claims of neuroscience grounding unsupported

strengths: Well-motivated architecture addressing genuine limitations in EEG modeling (time-frequency confusion, lack of spatial topology, scalability issues)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 9 diverse downstream tasks with both linear probing and fine-tuning, appropriate baselines including recent foundation models
Large-scale pre-training infrastructure with 28,000 hours of diverse EEG data from 9 public datasets demonstrating generalizability
Thorough ablation studies systematically validating contribution of each component (HFPM, DCM, TE, MoE)
Excellent reproducibility documentation including detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode, data descriptions, and promise of open-source code release
Consistent improvements across all 9 downstream tasks, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-class tasks (SEED, TUEV)
Scaling law analysis demonstrating positive relationship between model/data size and performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—individual components (time-frequency decoupling, topological embeddings, MoE, masked autoencoding) are established techniques; contribution is primarily in combination rather than fundamental innovation
Topological embedding mechanism insufficiently detailed and unclear how it generalizes to different electrode standards and montages despite claiming to 'unify different international standards'

Insufficient analysis of MoE specialization—claims about 'functionally specialized expert subnetworks' lack evidence; no visualization of routing patterns, load balancing, or ablation on number of experts
Performance comparisons mixed and sometimes unfavorable—on TUAB linear probing, Uni-NTFM (0.7844) underperforms LaBraM (0.8140); fine-tuned improvements often marginal; CSBrain comparison incomplete
Scaling analysis suggests potential over-parameterization—performance plateaus/declines for models >800M with 10k hours; missing scaling curves for smaller models with full 28k hours of data
'Interpretable representations' claim in abstract is unsupported—no evidence provided that representations are more interpretable than baselines beyond downstream task performance
Missing computational cost analysis—no training time, inference latency, or memory requirements reported; MoE inference overhead not discussed

Loss function design choices lack justification—time/frequency loss weights (λ_T=0.8, λ_F=0.2) appear arbitrary; no ablation; simple addition for topological embedding fusion (Eq. 7) not compared to alternatives
Limited analysis of learned representations—no separate investigation of what time vs. frequency streams learn; t-SNE visualizations are qualitative only
No statistical significance testing despite modest improvements in some settings; improvements averaged across 9 tasks in Figure 1 obscures per-task variation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 diverse downstream EEG tasks with consistent state-of-the-art results in both linear probing and fine-tuning settings
Clear and well-motivated problem formulation identifying three specific limitations of existing EEG models (decoupled coding, topological reconstruction, functional modularity)
Large-scale pre-training on 28,000 hours of EEG data from 9 public datasets with thoughtful data selection covering diverse paradigms (resting-state, emotion, cognitive, clinical)
Exemplary reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters (Tables 8-11), pseudocode (Appendix E), extensive supplementary analyses, and commitment to open-source release
Strong practical efficiency: MoE architecture achieves 1.9B parameter capacity with only 307M active parameters during inference, enabling scalability with manageable computational cost
Thorough stress testing and robustness analysis including missing channel handling (Table 18), cross-montage generalization (Table 19), and label efficiency (Table 21)
Systematic scaling law experiments (Tables 12-13) demonstrating proper performance scaling with both model size and pre-training data
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: HFPM is straightforward parallel encoding, DCM uses standard cross-attention, TE is hierarchical position embeddings, and MoE is established architecture—contribution is primarily in combination rather than algorithmic innovation

Neuroscience grounding claims are overstated: sparse coding invoked doesn't align with neuroscience definitions (confuses inference-sparsity with representation sparsity), decoupled coding justification lacks rigorous evidence, and topological embedding doesn't truly 'reconstruct geometry' but merely encodes discrete electrode positions

Unfair experimental comparisons: task-specific baselines (EEGNet, SPARCNet) trained on single datasets are compared against massive pre-trained model; fair comparison requires controlling for pre-training advantage or comparing primarily with other foundation models

Incomplete justification for design choices: Equation 7 uses direct addition of TE embeddings without exploring alternatives, frequency band definitions not specified despite being critical for reproducibility, and raw path contribution unclear beyond serving as reconstruction target

Questionable contribution of individual modules: MoE alone shows minimal isolated improvement (Table 4, A5: 66.23%), TE shows limited gains when ablated (Table 17: 0.24% improvement from Eabs), suggesting components may be less critical than claimed

Missing depth of analysis: no investigation of task transfer patterns, limited interpretation of learned specialization beyond visualization (Figures 6-8), absence of error analysis or failure case discussion, and no statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations

Limited scope of downstream evaluation: all 9 tasks are classification problems; generalization to regression, anomaly detection, or artifact detection tasks unclear; dataset sizes vary widely (28-2383 subjects) limiting absolute performance interpretation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 diverse EEG downstream tasks with multiple evaluation metrics and proper reporting of mean ± std
Large-scale pre-training on 28,000 hours of diverse EEG data aggregated from 9 public datasets
Thorough ablation studies in main paper and appendices covering component contributions, data augmentation, topological embedding variants, and label efficiency
Good reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset specifications, and promised code release
Multiple model scales (57M to 1.9B parameters) with scaling law analysis showing performance trends
t-SNE visualization demonstrates learned representations form more separable clusters compared to EEGNet and raw features
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: time-frequency decomposition is standard EEG processing; MoE Transformers established technology; dual-domain cross-attention is basic cross-attention. Contribution appears to be engineering recombination rather than methodological innovation

Weak neuroscience grounding: claims of being rooted in neural principles not substantiated; time/frequency separation is signal processing; topological embedding solves data heterogeneity not cortical geometry; MoE sparse routing is computational efficiency not biological emulation
Marginal empirical improvements: TUAB improvements of 0.25%, SEED of 0.19%, often within standard deviation ranges. No statistical significance testing to validate improvements
Unfair comparisons: 1.9B parameter model compared to 4-5M parameter baselines conflates size with architectural benefits. Lacks controlled comparisons with matched parameter budgets

Questionable design choices: raw path uses learnable projection as reconstruction target (circular design), critical hyperparameters (mask ratio 0.25, loss weights 0.8/0.2, expert count) lack justification or ablation

Topological embedding overclaimed: ablation shows 0.89% gain only, cross-montage validation on single scenario, intra-region coordinates never formally defined, claim to reconstruct brain geometry misleading
Missing statistical rigor: no significance tests, no hyperparameter ablations, performance plateaus at 800M parameters unexplained, results sometimes within error bars of baselines
Limited evaluation scope: all 9 tasks are EEG classification only; no other biomedical signals; no comparison with simple baselines like features+SVM; generalization claims overstated
Training costs not addressed: no discussion of GPU-hours for 28k hour dataset, memory requirements, or training efficiency—only inference costs reported
Shallow representation analysis: Figure 6-8 show expert usage patterns but lack interpretation; no attention visualization; no failure mode analysis; no investigation of what experts actually learn

strengths: Clear problem formulation with three well-articulated limitations of existing EEG models (decoupled coding, topological reconstruction, sparse modularity)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across nine diverse downstream tasks with both linear probing and fine-tuning settings
Large-scale pre-training dataset (28,000 hours from 9 public datasets covering diverse paradigms: resting-state, emotion, cognition, clinical, BCI)
Extensive ablation studies validating each component; HFPM provides largest gain (+6.9% AUROC); hierarchical TE necessity demonstrated (Table 17)
Thorough robustness and generalization analyses including missing channel handling (Table 18), cross-montage transfer (Table 19), and label efficiency (Table 21)
Scalable architecture with four model variants (57M-1.9B); MoE cleverly decouples capacity (427M params) from inference cost (74M active params, 15.87 GFLOPs)
Neuroscience-grounded design showing deep domain understanding with clear biological motivation for dual-stream processing, topological embeddings, and functional modularity
Consistent improvements over multiple baselines and competing foundation models across diverse tasks; strong performance on linear probing demonstrates representation quality
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode, dataset documentation, and promise of code release
Technically sound methodology with appropriate experimental design and no obvious technical errors
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty; individual components are established techniques (time-frequency decomposition, cross-attention, hierarchical embeddings, MoE) with novelty primarily in application and combination rather than fundamental innovations
Statistical significance not rigorously established; results reported as mean±std only with no formal hypothesis testing or confidence intervals; improvements often modest (1-5% on several tasks)
Small sample sizes on some downstream tasks (BCIC-IV-2a: 9 subjects, BCI Competition: 7 subjects) raise concerns about statistical power for observed improvements
Limited mechanistic analysis; while ablations identify important components, paper provides insufficient explanation of why components work and when they provide maximum benefit
Evaluation restricted to public datasets only; unclear how well findings generalize to proprietary/clinical EEG or real clinical deployment settings
Incomplete baseline comparisons; STFT baseline only tested on 2 datasets (Table 20); CSBrain results from published paper rather than reimplementation; ensures fair comparison challenging

Design choices underspecified and not ablated; frequency band selection not justified, five brain regions selected without ablation on granularity, Top-2 gating chosen without justification or k-ablation
Missing practical implementation details; no GPU memory requirements, training convergence speed, or inference latency (beyond GFLOPs) comparisons provided
Biological plausibility claims could be stronger; connections between model design and neuroscience sometimes superficial; MoE doesn't perfectly match sparse neural coding mechanisms

Cross-montage robustness evaluation limited; only high-to-low transfer evaluated (Table 19) on SEED; other montage combinations not explored; unclear if benefits generalize across different transfer scenarios
